name: Working practice for delivery teams
description: General practice for reviewing code, versioning, planning, releasing, handling incidents, debugging, accessibility, scaling and analysis; it is general practice, not a statement of how Moksy works.

cards.subject: A pull request
says: proposes a set of code changes for review before they merge
carries a description, a diff and the discussion about the change
cards.use: want a teammate to check a change before it reaches the main branch
not: merges the change automatically without any review

cards.subject: A draft pull request
says: signals that work is not ready for formal review
lets a developer share progress and get early direction
cards.use: want early feedback on an unfinished change
not: is merged automatically once the tests pass

cards.subject: A small pull request
says: limits a change to one purpose a reviewer can hold in their head
is reviewed faster and reverted more safely than a large one
cards.use: are about to open a change that touches many unrelated files
not: is only used for typo fixes

cards.subject: A pull request description
says: explains why a change is made rather than only what changed
tells the reviewer how the change was tested
cards.use: want reviewers to understand the intent of a change
not: repeats the diff line by line

cards.subject: A blocking comment
says: names a problem that must be fixed before the change can merge
cards.use: find a bug in a change that would break production
not: suggests a stylistic preference the author may ignore

cards.subject: A nit comment
says: flags a minor stylistic preference
may be ignored by the author without blocking the merge
cards.use: notice a small naming preference in an otherwise sound change
not: must be fixed before the change can merge

cards.subject: A review checklist
says: lists what every reviewer checks, such as tests, naming, security and error handling
cards.use: want reviews to be consistent between different reviewers
not: replaces the need for a human reviewer

cards.subject: Author-reviewer separation
says: keeps the person who wrote a change from being its only approver
cards.use: see an author approving their own change because the tests pass
not: lets an author merge their own change when the tests pass

cards.subject: Review turnaround time
says: measures how long a change waits for its first review
grows into a bottleneck when reviewers are overloaded
cards.use: notice finished changes waiting days for a first look
not: measures how long the author takes to write the change

cards.subject: A stale pull request
says: stays open long enough for its branch to drift from the main branch
raises the chance of merge conflicts
cards.use: find a change that has sat open for weeks while the main branch moved on
not: is one that has been merged and can be deleted

cards.subject: A commit
says: records a snapshot of changes with a message
forms the unit of history in version control
cards.use: want to save a set of changes with an explanation
not: creates a separate line of development

cards.subject: A branch
says: is a separate line of development that can later be merged
cards.use: want to work on a change without disturbing the main line
not: records a single snapshot of changes

cards.subject: A merge
says: combines the changes of one branch into another
cards.use: want the work from a finished branch to join the main line
not: throws away the other branch's commits

cards.subject: A merge conflict
says: arises when two branches change the same lines differently
must be resolved by a person before the merge completes
cards.use: find that git cannot combine two branches automatically
not: is fixed by git without any input

cards.subject: Rebasing
says: replays commits on top of a new base
rewrites commit history
cards.use: want a linear history before merging a branch
not: leaves the commit identifiers unchanged

cards.subject: A feature branch
says: isolates work on one feature until it is ready to merge
can grow long-lived and diverge from the main branch
cards.use: start work on a feature that will take several days
not: is the branch that always holds production code

cards.subject: Trunk-based development
says: keeps developers merging small changes to one main branch often
relies on feature flags to hide unfinished work
cards.use: want to avoid long-lived branches and painful merges
not: gives every feature its own branch for weeks

cards.subject: A git tag
says: marks a specific commit such as a release
cards.use: need a permanent name for the exact code that was released
not: moves forward automatically with each new commit

cards.subject: Git revert
says: creates a new commit that undoes an earlier one
leaves shared history intact
cards.use: need to undo a change that is already on a shared branch
not: deletes the earlier commit from history

cards.subject: Major, minor and patch numbers
says: number releases in three parts
raise the first part for breaking changes
cards.use: need to show from a version number whether an upgrade may break clients
not: are chosen by the marketing team for each release

cards.subject: A hotfix branch
says: carries an urgent fix to production outside the normal release cycle
cards.use: must ship a critical fix without releasing unfinished features
not: is created for every planned feature

cards.subject: Force pushing
says: overwrites remote history with local history
can destroy teammates' commits on a shared branch
cards.use: are tempted to force push to a shared branch to fix a mistake
not: is the safe way to add a new commit

cards.subject: A sprint
says: is a fixed-length period in which a team completes a planned set of work
cards.use: need a fixed rhythm for planning and delivering work
not: is an open-ended phase with no end date

cards.subject: A product backlog
says: is the ordered list of work a team may do
is reordered as priorities change
cards.use: need one place that holds every idea and request in priority order
not: lists only the work done in the current sprint

cards.subject: A sprint goal
says: states the single outcome a sprint aims for
guides trade-offs when scope changes mid-sprint
cards.use: must decide what to drop when a sprint runs short of time
not: lists every task in the sprint

cards.subject: A daily stand-up
says: is a short daily sync on progress and blockers
is not a status report for managers
cards.use: want a team to surface blockers early each day
not: is a long planning meeting for the next quarter

cards.subject: A sprint review
says: shows finished work to stakeholders to get feedback
cards.use: want stakeholders to see and react to what the team built
not: looks back at how the team worked together

cards.subject: A retrospective
says: looks back at how the team worked
produces improvement actions for the next period
cards.use: want a team to improve how it works together
not: demonstrates the finished product to customers

cards.subject: Velocity
says: measures how much work a team finishes per sprint
is a planning aid rather than a performance target
cards.use: need to estimate how much a team can take on next sprint
not: is a score used to rank individual developers

cards.subject: A story point
says: is a relative unit of effort estimate
is not a measure of hours
cards.use: need to compare the size of two pieces of work
not: equals exactly one hour of work

cards.subject: A WIP limit
says: caps how many items may be in progress at once
exposes bottlenecks by forcing work to finish
cards.use: see a board with many items started and few finished
not: caps how many items can be added to the backlog

cards.subject: A Kanban board
says: visualises work as cards moving across columns
cards.use: want everyone to see the state of all work at a glance
not: fixes the team to a time-boxed sprint

cards.subject: Definition of ready
says: lists what a work item needs before a team accepts it into a sprint
cards.use: find that half the sprint items are unclear when work begins
not: lists what must be true before work counts as finished

cards.subject: Scope creep
says: adds requirements to agreed work without adjusting time or budget
cards.use: watch a project grow with small unplanned additions
not: is the formal process for approving scope changes

cards.subject: A technical spike
says: is a short timeboxed investigation to reduce uncertainty
cards.use: cannot estimate a task because the technology is unfamiliar
not: is a full delivery of a feature

cards.subject: A meeting agenda
says: lists topics and desired outcomes before a meeting
cards.use: are about to invite people to a discussion
not: records what was decided afterwards

cards.subject: Meeting minutes
says: record decisions and actions rather than every remark
cards.use: need a short record of what a meeting decided
not: list the topics before the meeting starts

cards.subject: A decision log
says: records what was decided, by whom and why
cards.use: need to find out later why a past choice was made
not: lists tasks waiting to be done

cards.subject: An action item
says: names an owner and a due date for a follow-up task
cards.use: leave a meeting with something that must happen next
not: is a general topic that anyone may pick up

cards.subject: Timeboxing
says: gives an activity a fixed time limit
cards.use: see a discussion running far beyond its purpose
not: lets a discussion run until everyone agrees

cards.subject: An asynchronous update
says: shares information in writing so people can respond on their own schedule
cards.use: need to inform a team spread across time zones
not: requires everyone to attend a live call

cards.subject: A one-to-one
says: is a regular private conversation between a manager and a team member
cards.use: want a safe place to discuss workload, growth and concerns
not: is a meeting of the whole team

cards.subject: A working agreement
says: is a set of norms a team agrees for how it works together
cards.use: find that team members assume different rules about response times and reviews
not: is a contract with a customer

cards.subject: Psychological safety
says: is the belief that one can raise concerns or mistakes without being punished
cards.use: notice people hiding problems until they are too big to ignore
not: is a security policy for office doors

cards.subject: Project scope
says: defines what is included in and excluded from a project
cards.use: need to agree what a project will and will not deliver
not: lists the risks of a project

cards.subject: A milestone
says: marks a significant point of progress without taking time itself
cards.use: want a checkpoint showing a phase is complete
not: is a task that takes several weeks

cards.subject: The critical path
says: is the longest chain of dependent tasks that sets the minimum project duration
cards.use: need to know which delays will push back the end date
not: is the list of the most expensive tasks

cards.subject: A work breakdown structure
says: divides a project into smaller deliverables and tasks
cards.use: need to turn a large goal into estimable pieces
not: lists the people in a project

cards.subject: A stakeholder map
says: groups people by their influence and interest in a project
cards.use: need to decide how often to update each interested party
not: lists the tasks assigned to each developer

cards.subject: A RAID log
says: records risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies
cards.use: want one place to track what could go wrong and what is assumed
not: records only completed tasks

cards.subject: A project charter
says: authorises a project and states its purpose, scope and sponsor
cards.use: need formal agreement before a project starts
not: is the final report written at project close

cards.subject: A contingency buffer
says: adds time or budget to absorb uncertainty
cards.use: know an estimate rests on unproven assumptions
not: is padding hidden from the sponsor

cards.subject: A Gantt chart
says: shows tasks against a calendar with their dependencies
cards.use: want to see how task timings overlap
not: shows remaining work against sprint days

cards.subject: A burndown chart
says: plots remaining work against time
cards.use: want to see whether a sprint is on track to finish
not: shows task dependencies on a calendar

cards.subject: A range estimate for a project
says: gives a low and high figure instead of a single number
shows the uncertainty in the work
cards.use: are asked for a cost before the requirements are clear
not: gives one figure that is guaranteed

cards.subject: A change request
says: asks formally to alter agreed scope, design or a production system
cards.use: handle a stakeholder who asks for something outside the agreed scope
not: records a bug found in testing

cards.subject: A rollback
says: returns a system to its previous working version after a bad release
cards.use: respond to a release that is causing errors for customers
not: adds new features after a release

cards.subject: A feature flag
says: switches a feature on or off without redeploying
cards.use: want to release code now and enable the feature later
not: rolls back the database schema

cards.subject: A canary release
says: sends a new version to a small share of users first
cards.use: want to limit the damage of a faulty release
not: switches all traffic at once

cards.subject: A blue-green deployment
says: runs two identical environments and switches traffic between them
cards.use: want near-instant switchover and rollback between versions
not: sends a small share of users to the new version

cards.subject: Release notes
says: tell users what changed in a release
cards.use: are about to publish a new version
not: list every commit message verbatim

cards.subject: A change freeze
says: pauses non-urgent changes during a risky period
cards.use: approach a period when stability matters more than new features
not: blocks emergency fixes too

cards.subject: A smoke test
says: checks quickly that the most important functions work after a deployment
cards.use: need fast confirmation that a deploy did not break the basics
not: tests every edge case of every feature

cards.subject: A deployment pipeline
says: automates build, test and release steps in order
cards.use: want every change to go through the same repeatable steps
not: is a manual checklist kept in a wiki

cards.subject: A change advisory board
says: reviews higher-risk changes before they go ahead
cards.use: face a change that could affect many systems at once
not: approves every typo fix

cards.subject: An incident severity level
says: ranks an incident by its impact to decide the response
cards.use: must decide how fast and how widely to respond to a fault
not: ranks the engineers by experience

cards.subject: An incident commander
says: coordinates the response and makes the calls during an incident
cards.use: see several people investigating without anyone leading
not: fixes the fault personally

cards.subject: A status page update
says: tells customers what is affected and when the next update will come
cards.use: have an ongoing outage and anxious customers
not: describes the root cause in technical detail

cards.subject: Mean time to recovery
says: measures the average time to restore service after a failure
cards.use: want to know how quickly a team gets service back
not: measures how often failures happen

cards.subject: An on-call rota
says: schedules who responds to alerts outside working hours
cards.use: need someone reachable when a system fails at night
not: lists who attended last week's meetings

cards.subject: Alert fatigue
says: builds when too many low-value alerts cause people to ignore real ones
cards.use: see responders muting alerts because most are noise
not: is caused by having too few alerts

cards.subject: An incident mitigation
says: reduces the impact of a fault before the root cause is fixed
cards.use: need to stop customers being hurt while the real fix is still being built
not: is the permanent fix for the underlying cause

cards.subject: A root cause
says: is the underlying reason an incident happened rather than its trigger
cards.use: want to prevent the same incident recurring
not: is the first alert that fired

cards.subject: A service level objective
says: sets a target for how reliable a service should be
cards.use: need to agree how much downtime is acceptable
not: promises compensation to customers

cards.subject: An error budget
says: is the amount of unreliability an objective allows over a period
makes a team slow down releases when it is used up
cards.use: debate whether to ship another risky change after a bad month
not: is the money set aside to fix bugs

cards.subject: A reproduction case
says: is a reliable set of steps that makes a bug appear
cards.use: cannot fix a bug that only some users report
not: is the fix for the bug

cards.subject: A minimal reproducible example
says: strips a bug down to the smallest code that still shows it
cards.use: need to ask for help or report a bug to another team
not: is a copy of the whole application

cards.subject: Bisecting
says: halves the range of suspect changes repeatedly to find the one that introduced a bug
cards.use: know a bug appeared sometime in the last hundred commits
not: reads through every commit in order

cards.subject: A debugging hypothesis
says: is a testable guess about the cause of a bug
cards.use: have a symptom and want to narrow down the cause
not: is the confirmed explanation of a bug

cards.subject: Log levels
says: separate routine messages from warnings and errors
cards.use: need to turn down noise but keep serious problems visible
not: encrypt log files

cards.subject: Profiling
says: measures where a program spends time or memory
cards.use: want to find the real bottleneck before changing code
not: guesses which function is slow

cards.subject: A performance bottleneck
says: is the part of a system that limits overall throughput
cards.use: find that speeding up one component made no difference overall
not: is the fastest part of a system

cards.subject: Premature optimisation
says: spends effort speeding up code before measurement shows it matters
cards.use: see a team rewriting code for speed with no measurements
not: is the habit of measuring before optimising

cards.subject: The N+1 query problem
says: runs one query for a list and then one more query for each item
cards.use: see page load time grow with every extra row shown
not: joins all tables in a single query

cards.subject: Tail latency
says: describes the slowest responses, such as the 95th percentile
cards.use: find that the average is fine but some users wait very long
not: is the average response time

cards.subject: A load test
says: checks how a system behaves under expected or heavy traffic
cards.use: need to know if a launch will cope with demand
not: checks each function with one request

cards.subject: Cache invalidation
says: decides when a stored result is no longer valid
cards.use: see users given stale data after an update
not: removes the need for a cache

cards.subject: WCAG
says: is the set of guidelines for making web content accessible
cards.use: need a standard to check a website against
not: is a language for building web pages

cards.subject: Alternative text
says: describes an image for people who cannot see it
cards.use: add an informative image to a page
not: is the caption shown to every visitor

cards.subject: Colour contrast
says: is the difference between text and background colour that makes text readable
cards.use: find that grey text on a white page is hard to read
not: is the number of colours used on a page

cards.subject: Keyboard navigation
says: lets a person use every control without a mouse
cards.use: must support people who cannot use a pointing device
not: is only needed for games

cards.subject: A screen reader
says: reads page content aloud for people with little or no sight
cards.use: want to know how a blind user experiences a page
not: magnifies the screen for low vision

cards.subject: Semantic HTML
says: uses elements that describe their meaning, such as headings and buttons
cards.use: see a page built from generic boxes that assistive technology cannot interpret
not: styles elements with inline colours

cards.subject: A focus indicator
says: shows which element has keyboard focus
cards.use: find that keyboard users cannot tell where they are on a page
not: highlights the pointer position

cards.subject: A usability test
says: watches real users attempt tasks to find where they struggle
cards.use: want evidence about how easy a design is to use
not: checks the code for errors

cards.subject: A user flow
says: maps the steps a person takes to complete a goal
cards.use: need to see where people might drop out of a sign-up
not: lists the database tables behind a feature

cards.subject: A persona
says: is a representative profile built from research about a type of user
cards.use: want the team to design for a specific kind of person
not: is a real customer named in a case study

cards.subject: User-centred design
says: involves users throughout design and testing
cards.use: want design decisions based on user needs rather than opinion
not: lets the most senior person decide the design

cards.subject: A feedback loop
says: feeds the results of an action back to guide the next one
cards.use: want to learn from what customers do after a release
not: is a single survey sent once

cards.subject: A locale
says: combines a language and region that set formats for dates, numbers and currency
cards.use: must show a date and price the way a local user expects
not: is the physical location of a server

cards.subject: Internationalisation
says: prepares a product so it can support many languages and regions
cards.use: want to design software so adding a language needs no code change
not: translates the text into one language

cards.subject: Localisation
says: adapts a product to one language and region
cards.use: need to launch a product for a specific market
not: prepares the code to support any language

cards.subject: String externalisation
says: moves user-facing text out of code into translation files
cards.use: find text hard-coded in the interface
not: encrypts strings in the database

cards.subject: Pluralisation rules
says: vary by language, so a simple singular-or-plural test is not enough
cards.use: see messages like "1 items" in a translated interface
not: are the same in every language

cards.subject: Right-to-left layout
says: mirrors a page layout for languages such as Arabic and Hebrew
cards.use: must support a script that is read from right to left
not: only reverses the text colour

cards.subject: Pseudo-localisation
says: replaces text with altered characters to expose layout and hard-coded string problems
cards.use: want to find translation problems before real translations arrive
not: machine-translates the product into every language

cards.subject: Text expansion
says: describes translated text becoming longer than the source and breaking layouts
cards.use: see a button label overflow after translation
not: is the shortening of text when translated

cards.subject: Vertical scaling
says: adds more power to one machine
cards.use: need a quick capacity boost without changing the application
not: adds more machines to share the load

cards.subject: Horizontal scaling
says: adds more machines to share the load
cards.use: need capacity that can keep growing beyond one machine
not: adds more memory to a single server

cards.subject: A stateless service
says: keeps no session data between requests
can be added or removed freely behind a load balancer
cards.use: want to scale a service by simply adding copies
not: stores each user's session in its own memory

cards.subject: A load balancer
says: spreads incoming requests across several servers
cards.use: have several copies of a service and one public address
not: stores a copy of each user's data

cards.subject: Technical debt
says: is the future cost of choosing a quick solution over a better one
cards.use: see a quick fix making every later change slower
not: is money owed to a supplier

cards.subject: A dependency update
says: upgrades a library to pick up fixes and security patches
cards.use: learn that a library you use has a known vulnerability
not: removes the library from the project

cards.subject: A deprecation notice
says: warns users that a feature will be removed in a later version
cards.use: plan to retire an API that clients still call
not: removes the feature immediately

cards.subject: The expand-contract pattern
says: changes a database schema in backwards-compatible steps
cards.use: need to rename a column without downtime
not: drops the old column first and fixes the code afterwards

cards.subject: A data migration
says: moves or transforms existing data to a new structure or system
cards.use: must move customer records to a new database
not: copies only the application code

cards.subject: Backward compatibility
says: lets existing clients keep working after a change
cards.use: release a new API version that old clients still use
not: forces every client to upgrade at once

cards.subject: Capacity planning
says: estimates the resources needed for expected future demand
cards.use: expect a large growth in users and must avoid being caught short
not: reacts only after a system runs out of resources

cards.subject: Preventive maintenance
says: fixes problems before they cause failures
cards.use: want to patch and clean up regularly rather than after outages
not: fixes problems only after customers report them

cards.subject: A competitor analysis
says: compares rivals on offers, strengths and weaknesses
cards.use: need to see how an offer compares with others in the market
not: lists the company's own staff and skills

cards.subject: A case study
says: tells how a customer faced a problem and what result followed
cards.use: want evidence that a service works for people like the reader
not: is a technical specification for developers

cards.subject: A SWOT analysis
says: lists strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
cards.use: need a quick structured view of a company's position
not: ranks suppliers by price

cards.subject: A business plan
says: sets out an organisation's goals, market, offer and finances
cards.use: need to explain a business to a lender, partner or new team
not: is a list of next week's tasks

cards.subject: A value proposition
says: states the benefit a customer gets and why it beats the alternatives
cards.use: must explain in a sentence why a customer should choose a product
not: lists the features of a product in detail

cards.subject: A lean canvas
says: summarises a business idea on one page of nine blocks
cards.use: want a quick one-page view of a new business idea
not: is a detailed financial forecast

cards.subject: Requirements traceability
says: links each requirement to its design, test and result
cards.use: need to prove that every requirement was built and tested
not: lists the people who wrote the requirements

cards.subject: A stakeholder interview
says: gathers requirements by asking people with an interest in the outcome
cards.use: need to learn what a department needs from a new system
not: tests software with real users

cards.subject: A user story
says: describes a need from the user's point of view
cards.use: want to express a requirement in terms of a person's goal
not: lists the technical tasks to build a feature

cards.subject: Net promoter score
says: asks how likely customers are to recommend a product on a zero to ten scale
cards.use: want a simple measure of customer loyalty
not: counts the number of support tickets

cards.subject: An investor update
says: reports progress, numbers and needs to the people who funded a company
cards.use: must keep funders informed between funding rounds
not: is a pitch to a new customer

cards.subject: A due diligence review
says: checks a company's claims, finances and risks before an investment or deal
cards.use: are about to invest in or acquire a business
not: is an annual staff survey

cards.subject: A market segment
says: is a group of customers with shared needs
cards.use: need to decide which customers to focus on
not: is the whole population of a country

cards.subject: A coding standard
says: sets agreed rules for style and structure in code
cards.use: see every developer formatting code differently
not: is a list of approved tools to buy

cards.subject: A linter
says: checks code automatically for style problems and likely mistakes
cards.use: want style and simple errors caught before review
not: runs the full test suite

cards.subject: An architecture decision record
says: captures a design decision with its context and consequences
cards.use: must explain to a future teammate why a technology was chosen
not: lists every file in the repository

cards.subject: A README
says: is the first file that explains what a project is and how to run it
cards.use: set up a new project that others will open
not: is the license text of a project

cards.subject: A changelog
says: lists notable changes between versions for readers
cards.use: want users to see what is new without reading commits
not: lists every file changed in a commit

cards.subject: API documentation
says: describes an API's endpoints, inputs and outputs for its consumers
cards.use: expect other teams to call your service
not: explains the internal data model only to its authors

cards.subject: A code owners file
says: names who must review changes to given parts of a codebase
cards.use: want changes to sensitive code to reach the right reviewers
not: lists who wrote each line of code

cards.subject: Documentation drift
says: happens when documents no longer match the system they describe
cards.use: find a guide describing steps that no longer exist
not: is the habit of writing documents too early

qa.q: A developer wants a teammate to check a change before it reaches the main branch. What should they open?
qa.right: A pull request
qa.why: A pull request proposes changes for review before they merge.

qa.q: Which file is the usual first place that explains what a project is and how to run it?
qa.right: The README
qa.why: A README is the project's front door.

qa.q: What does alternative text do?
qa.right: Describes an image for people who cannot see it
wrong: Shows a caption to every visitor
Compresses the image to load faster
Adds a border around the image
qa.why: Screen readers read alternative text aloud.

qa.q: Which of these lists topics and desired outcomes before a meeting?
qa.right: An agenda
qa.why: The agenda comes before; the minutes come after.

qa.q: A team's sprint is running out of time. Which artefact should guide what to drop first?
qa.right: The sprint goal
wrong: The task with the most story points
qa.why: The sprint goal names the outcome the sprint is for.

qa.q: Two branches changed the same lines differently. What is this called?
qa.right: A merge conflict
qa.why: Git needs a person to resolve it.

qa.q: A release is causing errors for customers and a previous version worked. What is the fastest safe step?
qa.right: Roll back to the previous version
wrong: Add new features to the release
Wait for customers to stop reporting
qa.why: A rollback returns a system to its last working version.

qa.q: A manager wants each developer's velocity compared in the performance review. What is wrong with that?
qa.right: Velocity is a planning aid for a team, not a measure of individual performance
wrong: Velocity cannot be measured at all
Velocity only applies to Kanban teams
Individual developers have no velocity because they work in pairs
qa.why: Using velocity as a target invites gaming it.

qa.q: Why is it better to open several small pull requests than one large one?
qa.right: Each is easier to review and safer to revert
wrong: Large pull requests cannot be merged
Small pull requests skip the tests
Reviewers are paid per pull request
qa.why: A change with one purpose is quick to understand.

qa.q: A page loads slowly. A developer starts rewriting the biggest function without measuring anything. Which mistake is this?
qa.right: Premature optimisation
qa.why: Measure first with profiling.

qa.q: A team notices that finished changes wait days for a first review. Which measure describes this?
qa.right: Review turnaround time
qa.why: Turnaround is the wait for the first review.

qa.q: Users report that data looks stale after an update. Which problem is the likely cause?
qa.right: Cache invalidation
qa.why: A cached value was not refreshed when the source changed.

qa.q: A bug appeared somewhere in the last hundred commits. What is the efficient way to find the change that caused it?
qa.right: Bisect, halving the range of suspect commits each step
wrong: Read every commit message in order
qa.why: Bisecting needs only about seven steps for a hundred commits.

qa.q: A developer needs to undo a change that is already on a shared branch. Which command is the safe choice?
qa.right: git revert
qa.why: Revert adds a new commit and leaves shared history intact.

qa.q: A team wants fewer painful merges and gets by with feature flags for unfinished work. Which approach is this?
qa.right: Trunk-based development
qa.why: Small changes land on one main branch often.

qa.q: A page works with a mouse but a keyboard user cannot see where they are. What is missing?
qa.right: A visible focus indicator
qa.why: A focus indicator shows keyboard position.

qa.q: A translated button label overflows its box. Which concept describes the cause?
qa.right: Text expansion
qa.why: Translations are often longer than the source text.

qa.q: The message "1 items" appears after translation work. Which rule was ignored?
qa.right: Pluralisation rules vary by language
qa.why: A simple singular or plural test is not enough in many languages.

qa.q: A stakeholder asks for extra features mid-project without changing the date or budget. What is this called?
qa.right: Scope creep
qa.why: It adds requirements to agreed work without adjusting time or budget.

qa.q: What distinguishes a canary release from a blue-green deployment?
qa.right: A canary sends a small share of users to the new version; blue-green switches all traffic between two environments
wrong: Blue-green can only be used for databases
They are two names for the same thing
qa.why: The canary limits blast radius by exposure.

qa.q: An on-call engineer mutes most alerts because nearly all are false alarms. Which problem does this describe?
qa.right: Alert fatigue
qa.why: Too many low-value alerts cause people to ignore real ones.

qa.q: During an outage five engineers investigate in parallel and nobody tells customers anything. What is missing?
qa.right: An incident commander and a status page update
qa.why: Someone must coordinate and communicate.

qa.q: A service's average response time is fine, but a few users wait very long. Which measure shows this?
qa.right: Tail latency such as the 95th percentile
qa.why: Averages hide the slow tail.

qa.q: A list page runs one database query for the list and another for every row. What is this problem?
qa.right: The N+1 query problem
qa.why: Load time grows with every extra row.

qa.q: A team must rename a database column without downtime. Which approach is safest?
qa.right: Expand-contract: add the new column, move traffic over, then remove the old one
wrong: Rename the column during a quiet night and hope clients cope
Drop the old column first and fix the code later
Copy the whole database to a laptop
qa.why: Backwards-compatible steps keep old and new code working.

qa.q: A team cannot estimate a task because the technology is unfamiliar. What fits best?
qa.right: A short timeboxed technical spike
qa.why: A spike reduces uncertainty before estimating.

qa.q: Half the items in a sprint turn out to be unclear when work begins. Which practice would have prevented this?
qa.right: A definition of ready
qa.why: It lists what an item needs before the team accepts it.

qa.q: Why does a reviewer who is also the author's only approver weaken a review process?
qa.right: One person can pass their own work without a second view
wrong: The change cannot be merged at all
qa.why: Author-reviewer separation keeps a second pair of eyes on every change.

qa.q: A customer-facing outage is being handled. Which update is more useful to customers?
qa.right: What is affected and when the next update will come
wrong: The full technical root cause in detail
Nothing until the fix is deployed
qa.why: Customers need impact and a next update time.

qa.q: Why do teams keep decision logs?
qa.right: So the reasons behind a past choice can be found later
wrong: To track who attended each meeting
To measure how fast people type
qa.why: A log records what, who and why.

qa.q: A team wants to ship code now and enable the feature next week. What helps most?
qa.right: A feature flag
qa.why: The flag decouples deployment from release.

qa.q: Which statement about the critical path is correct?
qa.right: Delaying any task on it delays the end of the project
wrong: It lists the most expensive tasks
It contains tasks that can slip without consequence
It is the shortest chain of tasks
qa.why: It is the longest chain of dependent tasks.

qa.q: A team has used up its error budget for the month, and another risky change is proposed. What does the budget imply?
qa.right: Slow down risky releases and focus on reliability until the budget recovers
wrong: Ship faster to catch up on features
Raise the target reliability to compensate
qa.why: An error budget links reliability to release pace.

qa.q: A due diligence review finds that a company's headline customer numbers cannot be traced to any record. How should an investor treat the claim?
qa.right: As unverified, and ask for the evidence before relying on it
wrong: As true, because the company stated it
As false, and end the talks immediately
qa.why: Due diligence checks claims against records.

qa.q: Two translations of a product look correct to reviewers, yet a layout still breaks in production for one language. Which earlier check would have exposed it?
qa.right: Pseudo-localisation to reveal hard-coded text and layout limits
qa.why: It replaces text with altered, longer characters before real translations.

qa.q: Documents say the deploy takes three steps, but the real process has changed to five. Which problem is this, and what is the best fix?
qa.right: Documentation drift; keep the docs next to the code and update them in the same change
qa.why: Docs that change with the code stay accurate.

qa.q: A team demands a one-figure cost guarantee for a project whose requirements are still unclear. What is the most defensible response?
qa.right: Give a range estimate and state the assumptions
wrong: Give a single figure and add nothing
Double the figure and hide the buffer
qa.why: A range shows real uncertainty.

qa.q: A feature branch has been open for six weeks and the main branch has moved on. What is the best way to reduce the risk of the merge?
qa.right: Merge or rebase the main branch into it often, and split the work into smaller changes
wrong: Wait until it is finished and then force push
Merge it without review to save time
qa.why: Long-lived branches grow conflicts; small frequent merges shrink them.
